title: Plante v. Jacobs
summary: A substantially performing homebuilder could recover the unpaid price subject to appropriate defect deductions; replacing a misplaced interior wall was too wasteful when the wall caused no loss in market value.
notes: The accompanying notes question whether market price measures a particular homeowner’s actual loss. They discuss proof of personal value, intended repairs, and the owner’s likely use of an award. Those questions qualify the use of Plante as a universal market-value rule.

sections.Parties: Eugene Plante was the building contractor. Frank and Carol Jacobs were the owners who commissioned the house, withheld further payment, and challenged the amount of the builder’s recovery.
sections.Material Facts:
Plante agreed to furnish materials and construct a house on the Jacobses’ lot for $26,765. The owners paid $20,000. Disputes over workmanship and unfinished items led them to stop paying, and Plante did not complete all the work. He conceded omissions worth $1,601.95, including kitchen cabinets, gutters, a sidewalk, and other specified items. The owners identified roughly twenty additional defects and argued that strict completion would cost approximately one quarter to one third of the contract price.

The largest disputed item was a wall between the kitchen and living room, misplaced by more than a foot. Moving it would cost approximately $4,000 and require destroying completed work, with further plastering and decoration in two rooms. The house had already been decorated and occupied. There was no evidence that the owners demanded correction of that wall during construction. Experts for both sides agreed that its location did not reduce the house’s market value, although it frustrated the owners’ desire for a particular room size.
sections.Procedural History: Plante sued to establish a lien and recover the unpaid balance and extras. The trial court found substantial performance and allowed deductions for unfinished or defective work, generally using repair costs, but awarded no damages for the misplaced wall because it caused no diminution in market value. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed in 1960.
sections.Issue: Did the defects defeat substantial performance, and, if they did not, should the owners’ deduction be the cost of exact correction or the reduction in the house’s value?
sections.Holding: The contract was substantially performed. Repair costs were appropriate for separable defects that could be corrected without unreasonable destruction, but the misplaced wall was governed by diminution in value. The supported finding of no reduction in market value meant no damages for that item.
sections.Reasoning:
Substantial performance of a building contract depends on the nature and significance of what remains deficient. The court rejected a purely mathematical test based on the percentage of the price needed to achieve exact conformity. The owners had received a substantially completed house, so the builder’s entitlement to payment survived subject to compensation for defects.

The court then separated the defects rather than applying one measure indiscriminately. Repairs to cracks, the patio floor, and a nonstructural patio wall did not entail unreasonable economic waste. Moving the living-room wall would destroy completed work and damage surrounding construction, although it would add no market value. In those circumstances, the court treated the house’s lost value, rather than the cost of reconstruction, as the appropriate measure. This did not establish that the builder had complied exactly or that the owners’ preference was imaginary; it limited the monetary remedy for that breach.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This case separates three questions: whether performance is substantial, which defects are compensable, and how each defect should be valued. It links the conditions doctrine in Jacob & Youngs to the competing damages measures in Groves and Peevyhouse.

topics.remedies: Separates repair costs and diminution in value for distinct defects in one house.
topics.substantial-performance: The defects did not defeat the builder’s right to the contract balance, subject to deductions.
topics.interpretation: The specifications establish the promised house; remedial valuation is a separate inquiry.

mnemonic.rationale: A living-room wall a foot out of place
